title: Friday Night Lights
full_review:
"Friday Night Lights" (Universal) is a hard-hitting drama about a season in the life of a small-town high school football team battling to make it to the Texas state championship.

Based on the nonfiction best seller by H.G. Bissinger, "Friday Night Lights" is not just a "sports movie" -- though virtually every frame of the film involves football -- but an engrossing, at times unsettling, portrait of the lives and fragile dreams of young athletes and their families in economically depressed communities across America.

The film chronicles the real-life 1988 magic carpet ride of the Permian Panthers, a team out of Odessa, a dusty, football-obsessed town in the west Texas flatlands.

Director Peter Berg quickly establishes Odessa's boom-to-bust fortunes through tableaus of silent oil rigs and boarded-up storefronts, all shot in desaturated tones for added bleak effect.

Contrasting the barren landscape are the bright lights of Ratliff Stadium, site of a weekly autumn ritual where rabid locals can forget about their dead-end existences by living vicariously through the gridiron glories of their home-town heroes: among them, taciturn quarterback Mike Winchell (Lucas Black), cocky all-star running back Boobie Miles (Derek Luke) and fumble-prone tailback Don Billingsley (Garrett Hedlund) who suffers abuse from his drunken and bitter ex-jock father (played convincingly by country singer Tim McGraw).

Feeling the most heat is Gary Gaines (Billy Bob Thornton), the team's second-year coach who knows that his head will be the first to roll if the team fails to "win state."

The season starts off on a high note with a lopsided win. It proves a Pyrrhic victory when, on the last play of the game, the hotshot Miles suffers a serious knee injury, sucking the wind out of the team's sails. But as one would expect in this type of Cinderella sports story, the players find the heart to rise to the occasion in their quest for the Texas state championship. To win the Lone Star laurels they will have to beat a physically superior squad from Dallas in a David vs. Goliath showdown.

While not without its crowd-pleasing moments, "Friday Night Lights" differs from most feel-good sports movies in that it exposes the unpleasant side of high-stakes amateur athletics: an unhealthy pressure cooker where teens are asked to shoulder the expectations of entire communities and where coaches are paid more than teachers.

Football fans will find much to cheer about during the film's intense game sequences, which, though at times disorienting, are bone-jarringly realistic. Conversely, those who view football as ritualized violence may find themselves cringing through much of the movie. And while it is sometimes difficult to tell who's who under all the equipment, the frenetic camerawork keeps the audience so close to the action that helmets should be required for viewing (which would help muffle the ear-splitting soundtrack).

Unlike the book which delves deeply into the players' lives -- with detours into oil politics and race relations -- the film, while touching on those issues, keeps its narrative focus on the playing field. However, given the limited number of scenes where the actors are not in shoulder pads, the characters are surprisingly fleshed-out and several scenes are quite poignant.

Though some viewers may feel the film contains unfair stereotypes, others will applaud its emphasis on teamwork and personal excellence over winning. Opinions will also vary concerning a halftime scene where both teams pray the "Our Father" in their respective locker rooms as a prelude to another round of skull bashing.

While lacking the sociological scope of Bissinger's book, as a movie these "Friday Night Lights" shine brightly.

Due to much football violence, some underage drinking, two sexual situations, one with partial nudity, an abusive father-son relationship and some crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
